townhouse-share.html: In September 2026, 51.5% (1,837 of 3,570) of new residential dwelling consents were for multi-unit homes—with townhouses, flats, and units accounting for 36.6% (1,305) and apartments plus retirement village units accounting for 14.9% (532).

townhouse-share.source_html:

Source: Stats NZ — Building Consents Issued (Monthly Information Release) • Glossary: Turnkey vs Construction Loan • Derived by HLF Pulse (CC BY 4.0) • Checked: 22 November 2026. • Full Data Dictionary & historical series (/townhouse-share/) →

townhouse-share.definition: The percentage of monthly new residential dwelling consents issued for multi-unit homes overall (townhouses, flats, units, apartments, and retirement village units) and specifically for townhouses, flats, and units.
townhouse-share.formula: Multi-Unit Share = ((Total Consents - Stand-Alone Houses) ÷ Total Consents) × 100; Townhouse/Flat/Unit Share = (Townhouses, Flats & Units ÷ Total Consents) × 100
townhouse-share.hlf_interpretation: HLF market context: Compares the proportion of newly consented dwellings classified as multi-unit homes against stand-alone houses in Stats NZ's monthly release.
townhouse-share.methodology: Derived from Stats NZ Building Consents Issued by subtracting stand-alone houses from total new dwellings consented and dividing by total new dwellings consented, alongside the separate share for townhouses, flats, and units.
townhouse-share.summary_text: In September 2026, 51.5% (1,837 of 3,570) of new residential dwelling consents were for multi-unit homes—with townhouses, flats, and units accounting for 36.6% (1,305) and apartments plus retirement village units accounting for 14.9% (532).

rent-yield-pulse.html: In September 2026, New Zealand's national median weekly rent across newly lodged private tenancy bonds was $599/wk (up 1.5% year-on-year), with regional medians of $640/wk in Auckland, $580/wk in Wellington, and $560/wk in Canterbury.
rent-yield-pulse.official_data_summary: MBIE Tenancy Services (September 2026): National ('ALL') median weekly rent = $599/wk; Auckland = $640/wk; Wellington = $580/wk; Canterbury = $560/wk.
rent-yield-pulse.source_html:
HLF calculation: Reported national median = $599/wk; YoY = ($599 - $590) ÷ $590 = +1.5%
Source: Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) — Tenancy Services Rental Bond Data • Glossary: Gross Rental Yield • Derived by HLF Pulse (CC BY 4.0) • Checked: 22 November 2026. • Full Data Dictionary & historical series (/rent-yield-pulse/) →

rent-yield-pulse.data_type: Officially reported MBIE medians & HLF-derived YoY change
rent-yield-pulse.definition: The national median weekly rent across newly lodged private residential tenancy bonds in New Zealand, alongside regional medians for Auckland, Wellington, and Canterbury.
rent-yield-pulse.formula: YoY Rent Change (%) = ((Current National Median Rent - Prior Year Median Rent) ÷ Prior Year Median Rent) × 100
rent-yield-pulse.hlf_interpretation: HLF market context: MBIE rental bond medians measure the weekly rent agreed on newly lodged private tenancies during the month, rather than the average rent paid across all existing ongoing tenancies.
rent-yield-pulse.methodology: Extracted from MBIE Tenancy Services' monthly regional rental bond dataset (Location = 'ALL' for national median), with year-on-year dollar and percentage changes calculated against the same month a year earlier. MBIE bond statistics are compiled from new private tenancy bonds lodged during the reference month (excluding ongoing tenancies where no new bond is lodged, social housing, and tenancies without a lodged bond).
rent-yield-pulse.summary_text: In September 2026, New Zealand's national median weekly rent across newly lodged private tenancy bonds was $599/wk (up 1.5% year-on-year), with regional medians of $640/wk in Auckland, $580/wk in Wellington, and $560/wk in Canterbury.

rent-long-term-growth.html: Over the 10 years to September 2026, New Zealand's national median weekly rent on newly lodged bonds rose +53.6% (+$209/wk, or +4.4%/yr compound) from $390/wk to $599/wk. Over the past 5 years (from $495/wk), median weekly rent rose +21.0% (+3.9%/yr).

HLF calculation: 10Y Nominal: ($599−$390)÷$390=+53.6% (+4.4%/yr) | 5Y Nominal: ($599−$495)÷$495=+21.0% (+3.9%/yr)

total-housing-debt-stock.formula: Housing Share of Total Credit (%) = (Total Housing Lending ÷ Total Sector Lending) × 100; YoY Growth (%)

total-housing-debt-stock.methodology: Extracted live from RBNZ Table C5 (Sector lending). Computes year-on-year dollar and percentage growth and divides total housing lending by total private sector lending (housing, consumer, business, and agriculture).

mortgage-excess-repayments.html: In the September 2026 quarter, New Zealand mortgage borrowers made $4.30B ($4,297m) in voluntary excess mortgage repayments above their contracted minimum schedules (down 3.0% year-on-year from $4.43B a year earlier)—equivalent to 58.4% on top of the $7.36B ($7,361m) recorded in scheduled principal-and-interest repayments (and bringing rolling 12-month voluntary excess repayments to $18.03B).

HLF calculation: Quarterly Excess Repayments (September 2026 quarter) = $4.30B ($4,297m; 12M rolling = $18.03B) | Ratio to Scheduled P&I: $4,297m ÷ $7,361m = 58.4% (36.9% of combined scheduled + excess repayments)

mortgage-excess-repayments.hlf_interpretation: HLF market context: Under RBNZ Table C35's technical notes, 'other excess repayments' captures principal repaid above contracted scheduled payments—combining voluntary regular or lump-sum overpayments on table mortgages with net reductions in drawn revolving credit balances (while excluding full loan discharges upon property sale or refinancing).
mortgage-excess-repayments.methodology: Extracted live from RBNZ Table C35 (Residential mortgage loan reconciliation). fhb-share.hlf_interpretation: HLF market context: Measures first-home buyer share of new bank mortgage commitments (which in Table C31 are compared against total commitments across property purchases, bank-to-bank refinances, and equity top-ups by existing owner-occupiers and investors).
fhb-share.methodology: Derived from RBNZ Table C31 by dividing first-home buyer new lending value (LVRN.MMB1.AC1) by total new lending across all borrower types (LVRN.MMB1.AA). Mean loan size is LVRN.MMB1.AC1 (published by RBNZ rounded to the nearest $1m) divided by LVRN.MMB2.AC1.
fhb-share.summary_text: In September 2026, New Zealand registered banks committed 2,667 first-home buyer mortgages totalling $1.53B ($1,530m)—accounting for 20.3% of all new residential mortgage lending (up from 19.2% a year earlier), with an average commitment size of $573,678.

fhb-loan-size-gap.methodology: Derived from RBNZ Table C31 by dividing >80% LVR FHB lending value (LVRN.MMB1.BC1, rounded to $1m) by >80% LVR FHB loan count (LVRN.MMB2.BC1), and comparing against <=80% LVR FHB lending value divided by <=80% LVR FHB loan count. refinance.definition: The share of new residential mortgage lending value and number of commitments where a borrower switches from one mortgage provider to another ('change in loan provider' in RBNZ Table C33), alongside the mean refinanced commitment size.
refinance.formula: (Change in Loan Provider Value [LVRN.MMB1.AZD] ÷ Total Lending by Purpose) × 100; Mean Loan = LVRN.MMB1.AZD ÷ LVRN.MMB2.AZD

refinance.methodology: Derived from RBNZ Table C33 by dividing 'change in loan provider' lending value (LVRN.MMB1.AZD, rounded to $1m) by the sum of all purpose categories (property purchase AZC, top-up AZB, change in provider AZD, and other AZE). dti-headroom.data_type: Officially reported RBNZ series & HLF-derived >6x DTI share
dti-headroom.definition: The percentage of monthly first-home buyer mortgage lending value at registered banks committed at a Total Debt-to-Income (TDTI) ratio above 6x gross income, compared against the 20% RBNZ speed-limit cap on non-exempt owner-occupier lending.
dti-headroom.formula: (FHB Lending with TDTI > 6 ÷ Total FHB Commitments across all TDTI bands) × 100; Headroom = 20.0% minus (>6x Share)
dti-headroom.hlf_interpretation: HLF market context: RBNZ's 20% high-DTI (>6x) speed limit applies to each individual registered bank's new non-exempt owner-occupier lending flow (first-home buyers and existing owner-occupiers combined), not to the banking system as a single pooled allowance. Showing the system-wide first-home buyer >6x DTI share alongside the 20% benchmark illustrates aggregate positioning but does not establish an individual bank's available high-DTI headroom.
dti-headroom.methodology: Derived from RBNZ Table C40 by summing first-home buyer lending commitments in bands above 6x TDTI and dividing by total first-home buyer commitments across all reported TDTI bands in Table C40 (which differs slightly from Table C31 total FHB lending due to RBNZ rounding and DTI-unknown exclusions).

borrower-income.formula: Sum(Band Total Gross Income [$m]) ÷ Sum(Band Total Gross Income [$m] ÷ Band Average Gross Income [$k]) × 1,000
borrower-income.calculation: FHB: $383.0m total band income ÷ ~2,655 implied applications = $144,232 (±$500 band-rounding tolerance)
borrower-income.hlf_interpretation: HLF market context: RBNZ's Borrower Gross Income (BGI) measures combined application-level gross income across all borrowers on the loan (which for couples combines two incomes, and for investors includes personal salaries plus gross rental and other qualifying income). It does not measure individual solo salaries.
borrower-income.methodology: RBNZ Table C41 publishes official total gross income ($m) and average gross income ($000, rounded to the nearest $1,000) within each Total Debt-to-Income (TDTI) band rather than a single all-bands mean. HLF derives the overall band-weighted mean by dividing total gross income summed across all reported FHB TDTI bands by the implied number of applications (Band Total Income ÷ Band Average Income) summed across those bands. Because RBNZ rounds band averages to $1,000 and excludes DTI-unknown loans from Table C40/C41, the implied application count and reconstructed mean carry a rounding tolerance of approximately ±$500–$1,000 and differ slightly from Table C31 total FHB loan counts.

fhb-typical-dti.definition: The implied ratio of the national average first-home buyer mortgage commitment size (Table C31) to the band-weighted average first-home buyer gross application income (Table C41)—a ratio of aggregate averages rather than the mean DTI of individual borrowers—reported alongside the official share of FHB lending written at or below 5x and 6x Total Debt-to-Income (TDTI) in RBNZ Table C40.
fhb-typical-dti.formula: Implied Mortgage-to-Income Ratio = Avg FHB Loan (C31) ÷ Avg FHB Gross Income (C41); Share <= 6x TDTI = 100% − (>6x TDTI Share in C40)

fhb-typical-dti.hlf_interpretation: HLF market context: Dividing the Table C31 mean FHB loan by the Table C41 mean FHB application income produces an implied ratio of averages (and excludes non-mortgage debt such as student loans or credit card limits that banks include in actual TDTI assessments). The companion RBNZ Table C40 shares (<=5x and <=6x TDTI) measure the actual Total Debt-to-Income distribution of FHB lending commitments.
fhb-typical-dti.methodology: Divides the monthly mean FHB mortgage commitment size (RBNZ Table C31) by the monthly band-weighted mean FHB gross borrower income (RBNZ Table C41), paired with the official share of FHB lending dollar commitments in TDTI bands <= 5x and <= 6x from RBNZ Table C40. Small differences between Table C31 ($1,530m / 2,667 loans), Table C40 ($1,525.0m), and Table C41 (2,655.4 implied applications) reflect RBNZ band rounding and DTI-unknown exclusions.

net-worth-by-age-and-tenure.summary_text: In Stats NZ's triennial Household Net Worth statistics (year ended June 2024), median household net worth across all New Zealand households was $529,000—with households in owner-occupied dwellings recording a median net worth of $989,000 ($1,287,000 for mortgage-free homeowners and $727,000 for mortgaged homeowners) compared with $57,000 for households in non-owner-occupied dwellings (a ratio of 17.4x).

credit-card-limits-servicing-impact.definition: Total approved credit card limits across New Zealand registered banks ($ billions), the percentage of limits currently utilised, and the dollar volume of undrawn credit card limits.
credit-card-limits-servicing-impact.formula: Utilisation Rate (%) = (Total Advances Outstanding ÷ Total Credit Limits) × 100; Unused Limits = Total Limits − Advances
credit-card-limits-servicing-impact.calculation: Total Credit Limits = $20,835m ($20.84B) | Utilisation: $5,985m ÷ $20,835m = 28.7% | Unused Limits: $20,835m − $5,985m = $14,850m ($14.85B)
credit-card-limits-servicing-impact.hlf_interpretation: HLF market context: RBNZ Table C12 measures total approved credit card limits and advances outstanding across New Zealand personal and commercial cards. When assessing a mortgage application, lenders typically factor a percentage of a borrower's approved credit limits (rather than only the current balance owing) into expense calculations, though specific assessment rates and exceptions vary across lenders.
credit-card-limits-servicing-impact.methodology: Extracted live from RBNZ Table C12 by comparing total credit limits ($m) against total credit card advances outstanding ($m). Unused credit limit equals Total Credit Limits minus Total Advances Outstanding. RBNZ Table C12 includes both personal and commercial/business credit cards.
credit-card-limits-servicing-impact.summary_text: In September 2026, total approved New Zealand credit card limits in RBNZ Table C12 stood at $20.84B ($20,835m) with a 28.7% utilisation rate ($5.99B in advances outstanding)—leaving $14.85B ($14,850m) in undrawn credit card limits.

rent-vs-mortgage-interest-outgoings.html: In Stats NZ's year ended June 2025 Household Income and Living Survey (HILS) release, mortgaged households paying each component averaged $452.10/week in mortgage interest and $252.60/week in principal repayments (a combined component sum of $704.70/week, compared with Stats NZ's separately published $690.90/week overall average mortgage payment across all mortgaged households, while renting households paid an average of $505.50/week in rent), and across all New Zealand households housing costs averaged $22.30 per $100 of disposable income.

nz-median-house-price-quartiles.hlf_interpretation: HLF market context: Reports the 25th percentile (lower quartile), 50th percentile (median), and 75th percentile (upper quartile) prices of residential properties sold across New Zealand. Raw median and quartile sale prices reflect the mix of properties sold in the period and do not adjust for changes in dwelling size, type, or location composition.
nz-median-house-price-quartiles.methodology: Extracted live from the HUD / MCERT Property and Sales Statistics data download (.xlsx) and release dashboard (licensed under CC BY 4.0). Compiled from District Valuation Roll (DVR) freehold, arm's-length market residential sales supplied by Territorial Authorities through LINZ. Sales are recorded by agreement date (when the contract was signed) rather than settlement date; because DVR sales are transmitted after settlement, the series is published with a three-month lag and prior months are revised as late-settling sales are received.

gross-rental-yield-by-council.definition: Indicative gross residential rental yield across major New Zealand Territorial Local Authorities (city and district councils), derived by dividing annualised council median weekly rent on newly lodged bonds (MBIE Tenancy Services) by council median residential sale price (HUD / MCERT).

gross-rental-yield-by-council.hlf_interpretation: HLF market context: Provides a council-level ratio of annualised median weekly rent to median sale price across major New Zealand Territorial Authorities. Gross yield ratios do not deduct property operating expenses (such as council rates, dwelling insurance, maintenance, property management, vacancy, or mortgage interest) and do not represent net investment returns.
gross-rental-yield-by-council.methodology: Derived live by matching Territorial Local Authority (TLA) median weekly rents (MBIE By-TLA dataset) with TLA median residential sale prices (HUD / MCERT Property and Sales Statistics) for major urban councils. Note that MBIE bond rents and HUD DVR sale prices have different reporting lags (~6–8 weeks vs ~12 weeks) and reflect the separate samples of properties rented and sold in each district.
gross-rental-yield-by-council.summary_text: Combining MBIE Tenancy Services council median weekly rents (July 2026) with HUD / MCERT council median residential sale prices (July 2026), indicative gross residential rental yields across major urban councils were 3.61% in Auckland ($640/wk vs $921,000), 4.28% in Christchurch City ($550/wk vs $669,000), and 4.19% in Tauranga City ($690/wk vs $856,000).

hpi-low-vs-high-value-tiers.hlf_interpretation: HLF market context: Compares quality-adjusted annual price movements in the lowest valuation quartile (Q1) against the highest valuation quartile (Q4) within the MCERT House Price Index.
hpi-low-vs-high-value-tiers.methodology: Extracted live from the MCERT HPI composition series in the HUD / MCERT Property and Sales Statistics workbook and HPI composition dashboard. Properties are segmented into four equal value quartiles (Q1 lowest 25% to Q4 highest 25%) based on their relative rating valuation within their Territorial Authority.
hpi-low-vs-high-value-tiers.summary_text: In July 2026, the MCERT House Price Index for New Zealand's lowest valuation quartile (Q1 low-value homes) changed by -0.4% year-on-year, compared with -0.7% year-on-year for the highest valuation quartile (Q4 high-value homes)—a spread of +0.3 percentage points (while middle-quartile Q2 and Q3 homes changed by -1.1% and -1.0%, bringing the national all-dwellings composite HPI to -0.8% YoY).

insurance-claims-trends.hlf_interpretation: HLF market context: Summarises gross premium revenue, outwards reinsurance premium expense, net earned premium, and net incurred claims from RBNZ Table J10. Per RBNZ's survey notes, the Quarterly Insurer Survey covers 28 of 88 licensed insurers and reinsurers (representing just under 90% of sector assets and premiums) rather than a 100% market census, and outwards reinsurance expense covers all reinsurance cessions (not solely catastrophe cover).
insurance-claims-trends.methodology: Live-parsed from RBNZ Table J10 (Insurance Income and Expenditure workbook), subtracting outwards reinsurance premium expense from gross premium revenue to show net earned premium and comparing against net incurred claims. Covers the 28 general insurers in RBNZ's Quarterly Insurer Survey (~90% of industry premiums).

insurer-loss-ratios.methodology: Derived live from RBNZ Table J10 by dividing annual Net Claims Expense by annual Net Earned Premium Revenue across RBNZ's surveyed general insurer sample (28 of 88 licensed insurers/reinsurers, covering ~90% of sector premiums). Excludes non-claim underwriting, acquisition, and administration expenses.

equivalised-household-income-family-size.html: In the year ended June 2025, Stats NZ's Household Income and Living Survey (HILS, corrected series) recorded median annual equivalised household disposable income of $55,143 before housing costs (BHC) and $41,351 after deducting housing costs (AHC)—a difference of $13,792/year (25.0%) at the median—while mean (average) equivalised household disposable income was $63,397 BHC and $49,127 AHC (a difference of $14,270/year, or 22.5%).

nz-unemployment-rate.methodology: Extracted live from Stats NZ's quarterly Labour Market Statistics release and HLFS spreadsheets. Seasonally adjusted to remove regular quarterly calendar patterns. mcert-house-price-index-yoy.hlf_interpretation: HLF market context: Unlike raw median sale prices (which can shift when a higher or lower share of expensive homes sells in a given month), the SPAR-based MCERT House Price Index adjusts for property valuation quality and compositional mix across New Zealand.
mcert-house-price-index-yoy.methodology: Extracted live from the HUD / MCERT Property and Sales Statistics workbook and HPI dashboard. As detailed in the MCERT HPI Methodology Paper, the index uses a Sales Price to Appraisal Ratio (SPAR) method—comparing each property's sale price to its rating valuation (Capital Value) within each Territorial Authority and weighting by housing stock—to measure price changes while controlling for changes in the quality and mix of properties sold.
mcert-house-price-index-yoy.summary_text: In July 2026 (by agreement date), the official Crown House Price Index (MCERT HPI, calculated using the Sales Price to Appraisal Ratio methodology) changed by -0.8% year-on-year across New Zealand.

kainga-ora-first-home-loan-regional.html: In the Apr - Jun 2026 quarter, Kāinga Ora's 2,444 First Home Loan (5% deposit) approvals and 1,016 settlements across all 67 New Zealand Territorial Local Authorities were led by Auckland City (657 approvals [26.9%] | 277 settlements), Christchurch City (399 [16.3%] | 138 settlements), and Hamilton City (170 [7.0%] | 61 settlements). Across our Greater Wellington (HLF Subgroup)—combining Wellington City (87 approvals | 17 settlements), Lower Hutt City (31 | 27), Upper Hutt City (9 | 10), Porirua City (8 | 7), Kāpiti Coast District (11 | 5), and Wairarapa (17 | 7)—Kāinga Ora recorded 163 approvals (6.7% of NZ) and 73 settlements (7.2% of NZ).

Across our Greater Wellington (HLF Subgroup)—combining Wellington City (87 approvals | 17 settlements), Lower Hutt City (31 | 27), Upper Hutt City (9 | 10), Porirua City (8 | 7), Kāpiti Coast District (11 | 5), and Wairarapa (17 | 7)—Kāinga Ora recorded 163 approvals (6.7% of NZ) and 73 settlements (7.2% of NZ).

mortgage-market-share-timeline.data_type: Officially reported RBNZ C31 & C33 monthly series & HLF-reconciled 100% market share timeline
mortgage-market-share-timeline.definition: Full monthly percentage market share, dollar volume ($ millions), and loan commitment count (#) across New Zealand registered bank residential mortgages split by Borrower Type (RBNZ Table C31: First-Home Buyers, Other Owner-Occupiers, Property Investors, Business) and Loan Purpose (RBNZ Table C33: Property Purchases, Change in Loan Provider / Refinances, Equity Top-Ups, and Other), plus an HLF-reconciled 100% combined breakdown.
mortgage-market-share-timeline.formula: C31 Shares = Cohort ÷ C31 Total × 100; C33 Shares = Purpose ÷ C33 Total × 100; Combined 100% View partitions non-FHB Purchases (100% − FHB − Refinances − Top-Ups − Other) between Second+ Home Movers and Investors by their monthly C31 dollar ratio (OOO_Val ÷ [OOO_Val + INV_Val])
mortgage-market-share-timeline.calculation: Combined 100% ($ Value, September 2026): FHB 20.3% + 2nd+ Home Purchases 30.1% + Investor Purchases 8.9% + Refinances 22.9% + Top-Ups 12.8% + Other 5.0% = 100.0% (Top-Ups = 46.4% of loan commitments [9,639 of 20,763 loans], but 12.8% of dollar value [$962m of $7,533m])
mortgage-market-share-timeline.hlf_interpretation: HLF market context: Reconciles RBNZ Table C31 and Table C33 on a 0% to 100% monthly timeline so first-home buyers, home movers, property investors, bank-to-bank refinances, and equity top-ups can be compared over time without double-counting. Note that in standalone Table C31, total investor lending (~22% to 24%) includes investor refinances and top-ups alongside investor property purchases (~11% to 13%).
mortgage-market-share-timeline.methodology: Aligns every overlapping monthly observation from RBNZ Table C31 (Borrower Type) and RBNZ Table C33 (Loan Purpose) across both lending value ($m) and committed loan counts (#). Because Table C31 includes external bank refinances and equity top-ups inside Other Owner-Occupiers and Investors, the HLF Reconciled 100% view partitions total monthly lending without double-counting into: (1) First-Home Buyers (C31 AC1), (2) Second+ Home Purchases (non-FHB property purchases allocated by C31 Other Owner-Occupier dollar weight), (3) Property Investor Purchases (non-FHB property purchases allocated by C31 Investor dollar weight), (4) Refinances / Bank Switches (C33 AZD Change in Loan Provider), (5) Mortgage Top-Ups (C33 AZB Top-Ups), and (6) Other / Construction (C33 AZE).
mortgage-market-share-timeline.summary_text: In September 2026, across $7.53B ($7,533m) (20,763 loan commitments) in new New Zealand residential mortgage lending, the reconciled 100% dollar-value share comprised 20.3% First-Home Buyers ($1,530m), 30.1% Second+ Home Purchases, 8.9% Property Investor Purchases, 22.9% Refinances / Bank Switches ($1,729m), 12.8% Mortgage Top-Ups ($962m across 9,639 top-up loans, or 46.4% of all loan commitments by count), and 5.0% Other / Construction.

fhb-income-akl-vs-nz.methodology: Reports the five official RBNZ Table C41 first-home buyer TDTI band averages (TDTI <= 3, 3 < TDTI <= 4, 4 < TDTI <= 5, 5 < TDTI <= 6, and TDTI > 6), each band's official gross income pool ($m, rounded to $0.1m), each band's implied application count (Pool ÷ Average), and the HLF-derived overall weighted mean.

fhb-dti-above-6x.data_type: Officially reported RBNZ series & HLF-derived >6x DTI share
fhb-dti-above-6x.definition: The percentage of monthly first-home buyer mortgage lending value at registered banks committed at a Total Debt-to-Income (TDTI) ratio above 6x gross income, compared against the 20% RBNZ speed-limit cap on non-exempt owner-occupier lending.
fhb-dti-above-6x.formula: (FHB Lending with TDTI > 6 ÷ Total FHB Commitments across all TDTI bands) × 100; Headroom = 20.0% minus (>6x Share)
fhb-dti-above-6x.hlf_interpretation: HLF market context: RBNZ's 20% high-DTI (>6x) speed limit applies to each individual registered bank's new non-exempt owner-occupier lending flow (first-home buyers and existing owner-occupiers combined), not to the banking system as a single pooled allowance. Showing the system-wide first-home buyer >6x DTI share alongside the 20% benchmark illustrates aggregate positioning but does not establish an individual bank's available high-DTI headroom.
fhb-dti-above-6x.methodology: Derived from RBNZ Table C40 by summing first-home buyer lending commitments in bands above 6x TDTI and dividing by total first-home buyer commitments across all reported TDTI bands in Table C40 (which differs slightly from Table C31 total FHB lending due to RBNZ rounding and DTI-unknown exclusions).
fhb-dti-above-6x.summary_text: In September 2026, 9.0% of first-home buyer mortgage commitments at registered banks had a Debt-to-Income (DTI) ratio above 6x ($137.0m of $1,525.0m)—sitting 11.0 percentage points below the 20% RBNZ speed-limit allowance on total non-exempt owner-occupier lending.

top-up-share.formula: (Top-up Loan Commitments [LVRN.MMB2.AZB] ÷ Total Loan Commitments by Purpose) × 100; Mean Top-Up = LVRN.MMB1.AZB ÷ LVRN.MMB2.AZB

top-up-share.methodology: Derived from RBNZ Table C33 by dividing top-up loan commitment count (LVRN.MMB2.AZB) by total mortgage loan commitments across all purposes, and dividing top-up lending value (LVRN.MMB1.AZB, rounded to $1m) by top-up commitment count. RBNZ Table C33 counts committed loans rather than unique borrowers.

fhb-dti-headroom.definition: The percentage of monthly first-home buyer mortgage lending value at registered banks committed at a Total Debt-to-Income (TDTI) ratio above 6x gross income, compared against the 20% RBNZ speed-limit cap on non-exempt owner-occupier lending.
fhb-dti-headroom.formula: (FHB Lending with TDTI > 6 ÷ Total FHB Commitments across all TDTI bands) × 100; Headroom = 20.0% minus (>6x Share)
fhb-dti-headroom.hlf_interpretation: HLF market context: RBNZ's 20% high-DTI (>6x) speed limit applies to each individual registered bank's new non-exempt owner-occupier lending flow (first-home buyers and existing owner-occupiers combined), not to the banking system as a single pooled allowance. Showing the system-wide first-home buyer >6x DTI share alongside the 20% benchmark illustrates aggregate positioning but does not establish an individual bank's available high-DTI headroom.
fhb-dti-headroom.methodology: Derived from RBNZ Table C40 by summing first-home buyer lending commitments in bands above 6x TDTI and dividing by total first-home buyer commitments across all reported TDTI bands in Table C40 (which differs slightly from Table C31 total FHB lending due to RBNZ rounding and DTI-unknown exclusions).
fhb-dti-headroom.summary_text: In September 2026, 9.0% of first-home buyer mortgage commitments at registered banks had a Debt-to-Income (DTI) ratio above 6x ($137.0m of $1,525.0m)—sitting 11.0 percentage points below the 20% RBNZ speed-limit allowance on total non-exempt owner-occupier lending.

HLF calculation: FHB: $383.0m total band income ÷ ~2,655 implied applications = $144,232 (±$500 band-rounding tolerance)
Source: Reserve Bank of New Zealand — Residential mortgage borrower gross income (BGI) (Table C41) • Direct RBNZ C41 .xlsx • Glossary: Debt-to-Income (DTI) • Derived by HLF Pulse (CC BY 4.0) • Checked: 22 November 2026. • Full Data Dictionary & historical series (/borrower-income/) →

fhb-borrower-income.also_known_as: Borrower Gross Income (BGI) band-weighted mean across approved FHB applications (RBNZ C41, ±$500–$1,000 band-rounding tolerance)
fhb-borrower-income.source_full: Reserve Bank of New Zealand — Residential mortgage borrower gross income (BGI) (Table C41)

fhb-borrower-income.definition: The band-weighted mean annual gross borrower income across approved New Zealand first-home buyer mortgage applications and property investor applications at registered banks, derived from RBNZ Table C41.
fhb-borrower-income.formula: Sum(Band Total Gross Income [$m]) ÷ Sum(Band Total Gross Income [$m] ÷ Band Average Gross Income [$k]) × 1,000
fhb-borrower-income.calculation: FHB: $383.0m total band income ÷ ~2,655 implied applications = $144,232 (±$500 band-rounding tolerance)
fhb-borrower-income.hlf_interpretation: HLF market context: RBNZ's Borrower Gross Income (BGI) measures combined application-level gross income across all borrowers on the loan (which for couples combines two incomes, and for investors includes personal salaries plus gross rental and other qualifying income). It does not measure individual solo salaries.
fhb-borrower-income.methodology: RBNZ Table C41 publishes official total gross income ($m) and average gross income ($000, rounded to the nearest $1,000) within each Total Debt-to-Income (TDTI) band rather than a single all-bands mean. HLF derives the overall band-weighted mean by dividing total gross income summed across all reported FHB TDTI bands by the implied number of applications (Band Total Income ÷ Band Average Income) summed across those bands. Because RBNZ rounds band averages to $1,000 and excludes DTI-unknown loans from Table C40/C41, the implied application count and reconstructed mean carry a rounding tolerance of approximately ±$500–$1,000 and differ slightly from Table C31 total FHB loan counts.
fhb-borrower-income.summary_text: In September 2026, approved New Zealand first-home buyer mortgage applications at registered banks averaged $144,232 in combined gross borrower income (ranging from $123,000 to $197,000 across DTI bands, ±$500 rounding tolerance).

household-vs-individual-income-benchmark.html: In the June 2026 quarter, Stats NZ's Labour Market Statistics (Income) recorded median weekly individual income of $1,419/week ($73,788/year annualised) for people receiving wages and salaries, $962/week ($50,024/year annualised) across all people from all sources, and $959/week ($49,868/year) for self-employed individuals (with median full-time hourly earnings at $38.00/hour).

household-vs-individual-income-benchmark.hlf_interpretation: HLF market context: Provides individual-level median weekly and annualised income benchmarks from Stats NZ's annual June quarter income survey, distinct from combined multi-earner household or mortgage application income.
household-vs-individual-income-benchmark.methodology: Extracted live from Stats NZ's Labour Market Statistics (Income) June quarter release, multiplying official median weekly gross income figures by 52 weeks. As defined by Stats NZ, 'wages and salaries' covers both full-time and part-time employees, while 'all people from all sources' covers the wider working-age population (including part-time earners, government transfer recipients, and retirees).
household-vs-individual-income-benchmark.summary_text: In the June 2026 quarter, Stats NZ's Labour Market Statistics (Income) recorded median weekly individual income of $1,419/week ($73,788/year annualised) for people receiving wages and salaries, $962/week ($50,024/year annualised) across all people from all sources, and $959/week ($49,868/year) for self-employed individuals (with median full-time hourly earnings at $38.00/hour).
